item.title: National airline flies Cure Kids
item.description: NATIONAL airline Fiji Airways is helping Cure Kids Fiji extend healthcare programs, specialist training and research to communities nationwide, including remote maritime areas. Managing director and chief executive officer Paul Scurrah said the partnership reflected the airline’s commitment to supporting communities.
item.content:encoded:
NATIONAL airline Fiji Airways is helping Cure Kids Fiji extend healthcare programs, specialist training and research to communities nationwide, including remote maritime areas.

Managing director and chief executive officer Paul Scurrah said the partnership reflected the airline’s commitment to supporting communities.

“In a country of scattered islands, air travel is a lifeline, not a luxury,” Mr Scurrah said.

“Through our partnership with Cure Kids Fiji, we’re using that lifeline to help bring life-saving care closer to the children who need it.”

Since the partnership began, Fiji Airways has supported 41 flight sectors — 30 domestic and 11 international — enabling healthcare professionals, program staff, specialists and researchers to reach communities in need.

The initiatives have reached 819 people, including 716 pregnant women through antenatal programs and 103 children through rheumatic heart disease (RHD) screening.

Fiji Airways said the impact was evident at a community health screening during the Accor Hotels Sports Day in Nadi.

“Cure Kids Fiji and the Ministry of Health and Medical Services Western Division screening team offered free heart screening to families attending the event.

“Fiji Airways-supported travel enabled a paediatric registrar from Labasa Hospital to travel to Nadi to support the outreach. A total of 103 children were screened, with several identified as having early-stage RHD.

“Children with early-stage RHD often show no symptoms and may appear healthy. Early detection allows families to receive counselling and referrals for ongoing care before the disease progresses.”

Cure Kids Fiji country manager Dr Jimaima Kailawadoko-Matanaicake said the partnership was making a real difference.

“Something as simple as providing transport can completely change a child’s future,” she said.

With Fiji Airways support, Cure Kids Fiji is strengthening national programs including RHD prevention and screening, the Fiji Antenatal Study, Strep Vaccine Global Consortium research, the Fiji Oxygen Program, and climate and respiratory health initiatives.

Travel support has also helped teams reach remote areas such as Vanuabalavu, with improvements at Lomaloma Subdivisional Hospital supporting better service delivery.

The partnership will continue to support RHD screening, specialist training and research aimed at improving health outcomes for children.

item.title: Constitutional guides
item.description: Dialogue Fiji has launched two new publications to help Fijians compare recent constitutional frameworks. The publications are Recent Constitutional Frameworks: A Comparison between the 1997 Constitution, the Ghai Draft and the 2013 Constitution, and Understanding Recent Constitutions: A Citizen’s Illustrated Guide.
item.content:encoded:
Dialogue Fiji has launched two new publications to help Fijians compare recent constitutional frameworks.

The publications are Recent Constitutional Frameworks: A Comparison between the 1997 Constitution, the Ghai Draft and the 2013 Constitution, and Understanding Recent Constitutions: A Citizen’s Illustrated Guide.

Dialogue Fiji executive director Nilesh Lal said the publications aimed to shift debate from tribal politics and personalities to knowledge of provisions, noting that the test for any constitution was in how it protected rights and how it controlled power.

Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica said the publications did not tell readers which constitution was best and did not advocate for any amendments or replacements.

“They lay out what each constitution says, to allow citizens to compare for themselves,” Mr Kamikamica said.

“That restraint is not a weakness, it is the publication’s strength.”

He said that a constitution was a social contract, that legitimacy and public trust were inseparable from the openness of the process.

“Fiji has learned sometimes the hard way that a constitution handed out is a constitution contested, while a constitution built together is a constitution that can truly unite,” he said.

He said the process must belong to the people, not to any office, any party, or any individual, and when farmers in Tailevu, fishermen in Kadavu, market vendors in Ba and students in Suva all access the same information, the whole nation gets better.

University of the South Pacific Political Professor Dr Sandra Tarte said she found the shift from ethnic-based electoral rolls, which were a prominent feature of the 1970, 1990 and 1997 constitutions, to the common roll, which features in the Ghai Draft and the 2013 Constitution, particularly interesting.

“Also, the role of the President – from having certain legislative and executive powers under the 1997 constitution to a proposed advisory role in the Ghai Draft to being totally absent from the 2013 Constitution,” she said.

“We know of the debate around Section 131 of the 2013 Constitution which grants overall responsibility to the RFMF to ensure at all times the security, defence and well-being of Fiji and all Fijians. This has proved somewhat controversial as it may be interpreted as allowing the military a form of super constitutional authority.”

Dr Tarte said the value of the publications was that they gave Fijians the tools to make that judgment for themselves.

Both publications are now available to the public to support informed public discussion.

item.title: Tie-dye training empowers youth
item.description: YOUTH in Navosa are gaining practical tie-dye skills through a two-day training program aimed at helping them create products and explore small business opportunities. The training is being held as part of activities leading up to the Navosa Youth and Sports Festival, which will be held today and tomorrow at Vatureba Grounds in Navosa.
item.content:encoded:
YOUTH in Navosa are gaining practical tie-dye skills through a two-day training program aimed at helping them create products and explore small business opportunities.

The training is being held as part of activities leading up to the Navosa Youth and Sports Festival, which will be held today and tomorrow at Vatureba Grounds in Navosa.

Participants are learning hands-on techniques for producing tie-dye products, with the skills intended to help them develop creative and entrepreneurial opportunities within their communities.

The initiative also aims to strengthen skills of rural youth and encourage greater economic participation by providing practical knowledge that can be applied to small-scale income generating activities.

The training forms part of wider efforts to provide young people with opportunities to develop skills that can support their livelihoods and contribute to their communities.

item.title: Waqa praises Fiji’s PIF contribution
item.description: FIJI made strong contributions to discussions at the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Foreign Ministers Meeting, according to PIFs General Secretary Baron Waqa. Mr Waqa said Fiji’s representatives highlighted key issues Pacific leaders need to address ahead of upcoming regional and international meetings.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI made strong contributions to discussions at the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Foreign Ministers Meeting, according to PIFs General Secretary Baron Waqa.

Mr Waqa said Fiji’s representatives highlighted key issues Pacific leaders need to address ahead of upcoming regional and international meetings.

He said Fiji had contributed significantly to discussions during the meeting, with its views helping highlight issues that need continued attention and preparation.

“Fiji has always been active, and let me say this, that this is a Pacific pre-COP with Australia – Australia and the Pacific in partnership,” Mr Waqa said.

“Fiji is hosting the pre-COPs meeting, and then Tuvalu is on the side. Fiji today contributed very well.”

Mr Waqa said Pacific countries were working together to ensure leaders were prepared for discussions on issues including health, education and disability inclusion.

He said several legal frameworks would also remain part of the discussions, acknowledging that reaching agreement on such issues would not always be easy.

Mr Waqa also referred to ongoing discussions on a proposed security treaty involving the Solomon Islands.

He said the various issues needed to be carefully considered and clearly understood by Pacific leaders as the region worked towards agreed outcomes.

item.title: New market laws to ban sales of meat, fish and mixed kava
item.description: The sale of prohibited meat and fish and mixed kava will be forbidden in municipal markets across Fiji under proposed new regulations endorsed by Cabinet. The restrictions are among key changes arising from a review of the Market By-Laws under the Local Government Act 1972, with new Local Government (Municipal Market) Regulations now set to be drafted.
item.content:encoded:
The sale of prohibited meat and fish and mixed kava will be forbidden in municipal markets across Fiji under proposed new regulations endorsed by Cabinet.

The restrictions are among key changes arising from a review of the Market By-Laws under the Local Government Act 1972, with new Local Government (Municipal Market) Regulations now set to be drafted.

Under the proposed framework, municipal, mini and satellite markets will operate under more consistent rules, including tighter controls over products offered for sale.

The regulations will specifically prohibit the sale of prohibited meat and fish, while the sale of mixed kava will also be banned.

Wholesale activities within markets will also be prohibited.

The changes form part of wider efforts to strengthen health and food safety standards and provide greater protection for consumers and vendors.

Cooked food vendors operating from markets will be required to comply with applicable food safety and health standards.

The new regulations will also require vendors to display prices in writing, aimed at providing consumers with greater transparency over the prices they are being charged.

Other changes will cover market operating arrangements, dispute resolution, fee and revenue collection, environmental management and accountability in the operation of markets.

The proposed regulations are intended to establish a standard framework for market operations across Fiji, replacing differing practices with consistent requirements for vendors and market authorities.

item.title: Minister’s call to graduates
item.description: HEALTH Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu has urged dental graduates still without public-sector placements to approach the ministry directly, as some junior dentists say they have been waiting up to 15 months for employment. “They should just come to HQ and talk with our human resources department,” Dr Lalabalavu told The Fiji Times.
item.content:encoded:
HEALTH Minister Dr Atonio Lalabalavu has urged dental graduates still without public-sector placements to approach the ministry directly, as some junior dentists say they have been waiting up to 15 months for employment.

“They should just come to HQ and talk with our human resources department,” Dr Lalabalavu told The Fiji Times.

“Or even come up to my office and I can talk with them and see how best we can address their issues.”

The call comes as graduates from the 2023-2024 cohort say they remain unemployed despite completing five-year Bachelor of Dental Surgery degrees, mandatory one-year internships and registration with the Fiji Medical and Dental Council.

“Despite completing all required education and training, many of us have now remained unemployed for approximately 14–15 months since completing our internship,” they said.

The graduates said some had found only inconsistent work in private practices while waiting for public-sector positions.

The 2024 cohort, which completed internships in March 2026, is also awaiting placements after sitting Dental Officer interviews that month. The vacancies were first advertised in December 2025.

The situation has also affected National Toppers Scheme recipients, who are bonded to serve Fiji for seven and a half years but say some have completed only one year of service.

Fiji Dental Association president Dr Parikshath Naidu said the association was aware of graduates struggling to find work but did not have official unemployment figures.

“We have assisted where we could by supporting their registration, sharing advice and looking for job vacancies,” he said.

The association said workforce planning should prioritise basic dental care and employment for local graduates before expanding specialist services.

item.title: Ratu Eparama remembered for lifelong service
item.description: THE late Tui Vuda Ratu Eparama Kitione Tavaiqia has been remembered as a dedicated soldier, chief and community leader who served his people and Fiji with distinction. Speaking at his funeral, Captain Savenaca Degei said Ratu Eparama answered the call by the late Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna to young Fijian men to join the military, despite his elders wanting him to remain in Vuda and look after the land.
item.content:encoded:
THE late Tui Vuda Ratu Eparama Kitione Tavaiqia has been remembered as a dedicated soldier, chief and community leader who served his people and Fiji with distinction.

Speaking at his funeral, Captain Savenaca Degei said Ratu Eparama answered the call by the late Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna to young Fijian men to join the military, despite his elders wanting him to remain in Vuda and look after the land.

Ratu Eparama joined the Republic of the Fiji Military Forces in 1951 and was deployed to the Malaya Campaign with the First Battalion Fiji Infantry Regiment aboard the Asturias on January 8, 1952.

“He was not merely a soldier by title, he was a soldier by character, discipline, resilient and committed to the task entrusted to him,” Capt Degei said.

Speaking for the Vanua of Vuda, Taukei Nakelo Ratu Josaia Natakele said the late chief remained steadfast in his leadership throughout his life.

“He was 95 but he was still planting sugar cane,” he said.

“He had businesses, he was committed to the work of the church and led and inspired our people.”

Tui Nawaka Ratu Joeli Bulu Derenalagi said Ba would remember Ratu Eparama as a voice of calm during difficult times.

The eighth chief installed through Vuda’s traditional chiefly succession, Ratu Eparama’s tenure included developments such as a new two-storey, eight-classroom building at Vuda District School and efforts towards relocating the military camp to Kubunasarava.

His passing marks the end of an era for the Vanua o Vuda.
